title: What happens in read()?
question: A program reads 64 bytes of a file. Which parts of the kernel does that go through? (Here the file is in memory: no disk.)
text: A program reads 64 bytes of a file. The bytes go through three layers, and here the file is in memory, so no disk is involved.
1. [ksys_read](2:ksys_read) is the syscall's entry: the fd turns into the open file (a `struct file`) and the position to read at, which starts at 0.
2. [vfs_read](2:vfs_read) is the VFS, the same for every file system: is the file open for reading, is the range sane, then it calls the file system's own read.

3. [filemap_read](2:filemap_read) is the page cache: a file's data lives in memory pages. Find the page at the position, copy from it to the program's buffer. In ramfs the pages are all the file is, so this is where the bytes come from.

[What it stored](2:ksys_read:stores): the file's position, the count read. [What filemap_read changed](2:filemap_read:objects): the read's position (the `kiocb`'s `ki_pos`, 0 to 18), the page's reference count, the inode's access time; and the page is the inode's (its `mapping`). The Stack shows `count` and `buf`. Try: [read twice](try:1): the position has moved, so the second read returns 0, the end of the file; or [4 bytes at a time](try:2).
tries: char buf[64]; int fd = openat(AT_FDCWD, "/note.txt", O_RDONLY); read(fd, buf, 64); read(fd, buf, 64); close(fd)
char buf[4]; int fd = openat(AT_FDCWD, "/note.txt", O_RDONLY); read(fd, buf, 4); read(fd, buf, 4); close(fd)
